title:
Atmospheric
Removal
of Nitrous Oxide: Approaches and
Feasibility
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nitrous oxide (N2O) is the third-largest contributor to anthropogenic greenhouse gas forcing and the dominant anthropogenic ozone-depleting emission. While mitigation can flatten emissions, there is no clear pathway to eliminate residual emissions from agriculture and other diffuse sources, a key challenge for climate stabilization. The potential role of atmospheric removal has not been holistically assessed, yet N2O’s high potency and long atmospheric lifetime indicate the potential for a durable climate benefit. This review synthesizes emerging approaches for atmospheric N2O removal, organized by reaction mechanism (thermal destruction and thermocatalysis, photolysis, gas-phase radical reactions, photocatalysis, and biological reduction) and deployment format (closed versus open system). Each is evaluated for technical efficacy, climate viability, environmental and social viability, and economic plausibility using lower-bound cost models. No approach yet satisfies all four: gas-phase radical reactors are precluded by their kinetics, thermocatalytic and photocatalytic reactors require ten- to hundred-fold performance gains, and open-system approaches have the lowest cost floors but face the greatest measurement and governance challenges. These results identify the performance thresholds and broader constraints that govern feasibility across pathways, providing a foundation for a research agenda and for assessing the role of N2O removal alongside emissions mitigation.</jats:p>

title:
Toward Rational
Design of Low-Salt-Rejection Reverse
Osmosis for Minimal and Zero Liquid Discharge

affiliation.name: China University of Mining and Technology (Beijing) , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Low-salt-rejection reverse osmosis (LSRRO) has emerged as a promising technology for concentrating high-salinity brines in minimal- and zero-liquid-discharge (MLD/ZLD) applications. However, rational LSRRO design remains hindered by uncertainties about how existing modeling frameworks should be interpreted and applied. In this Perspective, we critically examine the limitations of process modeling and module-scale analysis in LSRRO design. Conventional process models can yield misleading predictions for spiral-wound LSRRO modules because the stagewise concentration cutoff embedded in these models is based on the cumulative permeate composition rather than the local permeate conditions that govern water transport. Experimental results and local transport calculations show that the brine concentration in spiral-wound LSRRO stages is not constrained by a fixed thermodynamic concentration cutoff. Nevertheless, standalone process models remain inherently limited in assessing practical feasibility because they do not resolve kinetic constraints, such as declining water flux along the module. Module-scale analysis is therefore essential for linking local transport behavior to practical design metrics, including membrane area requirements, productivity, and achievable brine concentration. However, its predictive accuracy is constrained because transport parameters derived from conventional local transport models vary with salinity, which challenges their use as constants across the module. This Perspective therefore highlights the need for condition-dependent and experimentally validated local transport descriptions to enable rational LSRRO design for future MLD/ZLD applications.</jats:p>

title:
Dynamic Nature of
Soil Iron Minerals: Recent Advances
Using Iron Isotope Tracers and Mössbauer Spectroscopy

affiliation.name: Netherlands Organization of Applied Scientific Research (TNO) , , Princetonlaan 6 , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Iron plays a central role in defining the redox and surface chemical environment of soils and sediments, by mediating the behavior of nutrients, pollutants, and carbon compounds. However, the mechanisms that drive dynamic changes in Fe speciation and mineral composition can be difficult to trace. Over three decades, technical advances in spectroscopy and theoretical modeling techniques have revealed detailed mechanisms of Fe mineral recrystallization and transformation. Here, we provide a perspective on the application of iron isotopic tracers to the development of atomic-scale mechanistic understanding of Fe mineral dynamics. We review key milestones in the advancement of 57Fe tracers coupled with 57Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy and draw links between the understanding of Fe dynamics with 57Fe tracers and biogeochemical cycling of other elements in soils and sediments. Iron isotopes are increasingly used in Fe biogeochemistry research, and our analysis will point out unique opportunities offered by 57Fe tracers to unravel important questions in soil biogeochemistry today.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The effect of prenatal organophosphate esters (OPEs) exposure on offspring reproductive development and the potential role of the placenta remain unclear. We investigated the associations of prenatal OPE exposure with the second-to-fourth digit ratio (2D:4D) and the mediating role of placental DNA methylation (DNAm) levels of PPAR pathway genes. Maternal urine OPE metabolites at 12–16 gestational weeks were measured. Placental DNAm levels at birth and children’s 2D:4D at ages 4 and 6 years were assessed. Multiple linear regression, BKMR, and causal mediation analyses were applied. We observed associations between prenatal exposure to BBOEP, BEHP, DBP, and DPP and increased 2D:4D in boys, whereas DBP and DCP were associated with decreased 2D:4D in girls. BKMR identified alkyl-OPEs, particularly BBOEP, as the primary contributors in boys. Moreover, hypermethylation of RXRA, ACAA1, and ACADM was associated with decreased 2D:4D in all populations. In girls, the associations among higher OPE exposure, increased ACAA1 methylation, and lower 2D:4D suggested a potential mediation pathway, while the mediation effects were not statistically significant. These findings suggest sex-specific associations between prenatal OPE exposure and 2D:4D. The potential role of placental PPAR-related DNAm in these associations warrants further investigation.</jats:p>

title: Medium-Entropy LDH-Driven Electronic Coupling of MnO x for Preferential Oxidation of Formaldehyde
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Preferential oxidation of formaldehyde (HCHO) in natural gas engine exhaust is pivotal to prevent NH3–SCR catalyst deactivation and inhibit highly toxic hydrogen cyanide (HCN) formation. Although manganese-based catalysts exhibit prominent activity for HCHO oxidation, complete mineralization is still hindered by poor electron-transfer efficiency and insufficient reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Herein, we fabricate hierarchical medium-entropy LDH nanoflower-anchored MnOx catalysts (MnO2@NiMgAl-MELH) via a facile in situ growth strategy, enabling 100% mineralization of HCHO at room temperature. Structural characterizations and DFT calculations verify that Ni–Mn electronic coupling optimizes the electronic structure, facilitates charge transfer, reduces oxygen vacancy formation energy, and boosts O2 and H2O activation to generate abundant ROS (O2–, O22–, and surface −OH). Furthermore, in situ DRIFTS confirms that ROS synergistically accelerate HCHO and formate intermediate oxidation, achieving complete mineralization of HCHO. This work develops a low-cost and high-performance catalyst for HCHO preferential oxidation and offers a broadly applicable strategy for air pollutant purification.</jats:p>

title:
PFAS
in Follicular Fluid, Anti-Müllerian Hormone,
and Oocyte Developmental Competence: A Prospective Study in GIVES

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this prospective study based on the Guangxi In Vitro Fertilization and the Environment Study (GIVES) cohort, we measured poly- and perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in the ovarian follicular fluid of 729 participants to investigate their association with oocyte developmental competence. The PFAS mixture was negatively associated with Metaphase II (MII) oocyte rate, with chlorinated polyfluoroalkyl ether sulfonic acids (Cl-PFESAs) identified as the primary contributor in Bayesian kernel machine regression (BKMR) models. Cl-PFESAs were negatively associated with oocyte maturation [relative risk (RR) = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.56–0.79], fertilization (RR = 0.78, 95% CI: 0.67–0.90), blastocyst formation (RR = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.70–0.94), and high-quality blastocyst formation (RR = 0.49, 95% CI: 0.41–0.58). Serum anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) may act as a key modifier, with a stronger association observed in women with low AMH for MII oocyte rate [relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI) = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.12–0.54] and fertilization rate (RERI = 0.24, 95% CI: 0.003–0.49). Our findings indicate that PFAS, particularly Cl-PFESAs, in follicular fluid are linked to impaired oocyte developmental competence, with AMH serving as a potential modifier. Further studies are warranted to validate our findings and assess the implications of PFAS for reproductive outcomes.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The plant-beneficial bacterium Bacillus velezensis and related Bacillus species are increasingly recognized as important contributors to plant growth and health, yet the ecological functions of their secondary metabolites in situ remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how lipopeptides produced by Bacillus species influence plant performance and root-associated microbial communities. Using Arabidopsis thaliana as a model host, we show that bacterial lipopeptides produced during root colonization promote plant growth by enhancing the uptake of essential mineral elements, including magnesium, calcium, iron, and zinc. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that lipopeptides upregulated host genes involved in metal transport and homeostasis in roots, while downregulating negative regulators of metal uptake. The lipopeptide production reshaped the composition of root-associated bacterial communities by increasing the relative abundance of putatively beneficial taxa and altering overall rhizosphere community structure. Functional genes indicated that lipopeptide enrichment was associated with microbial pathways related to metal transport, nutrient acquisition, and stress adaptation, suggesting that lipopeptides modulate both plant and microbial traits relevant to nutrient cycling. These results provide new insight into the ecological roles of B. velezensis-derived metabolites in plant-associated microbiomes and highlight lipopeptides as promising targets for harnessing beneficial plant–microbe interactions in sustainable agriculture.</jats:p>

title:
Long-Term
Biogeochemical
Stabilization of Carbonate-Bearing
Pb–Zn–Cu Mine Tailings by Amendment-Assisted Phytostabilization

affiliation.name: Missouri University of Science and Technology , , , ,
Missouri University of Science and Technology , , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Legacy Pb–Zn–Cu mine tailings can remain barren and geochemically reactive for decades. Although amendment-assisted revegetation can establish short-term plant growth, sustained phytostabilization requires metal attenuation and soil-like development over years after amendment-derived nutrients and organic matter decline. We evaluated seven-year biogeochemical stabilization of carbonate-bearing tailings planted with the native legume Dalea purpurea. Biosolids (BS), biochar (BC), and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) were incorporated into the upper 8 cm, while the underlying 12 cm remained unamended. Tailings pore water was monitored annually, and year-seven cores were analyzed by depth for organic carbon, PLFA-based microbial indicators, aqua-regia-extractable metals, sequential metal fractionation, and X-ray diffraction. Biosolids initially increased EC, DOC, DN, and dissolved Pb, Zn, and Cu, whereas BC- and/or AMF-containing treatments showed greater long-term reductions in dissolved metal concentrations. AMF-inoculated treatments increased organic carbon and microbial biomass indicators below the amended layer, while deeper root penetration was also observed, consistent with profile-scale biological development. Sequential extraction showed metal-specific repartitioning: Pb was primarily carbonate- and Fe/Mn oxide-associated; Zn remained partly carbonate-linked; and Cu shifted toward organic/sulfide-associated and residual pools, consistent with lower relative lability. These findings show that surface-applied amendment and planting strategies can promote coupled biological and geochemical stabilization in initially unamended deeper tailings layers, supporting ecosystem restoration beyond short-term surface revegetation.</jats:p>

title:
Surface
Chemistry
Shapes Nanoplastic Mixture Responses
in Developing Amniote Embryos

affiliation.name: The University of North Texas , , 1155 Union Circle , , ,

Southern University of Science and Technology , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nanoplastics (NPs) are an emerging environmental concern, yet their developmental impacts on terrestrial amniotes and their mixture effects are only beginning to be understood. Using a chicken embryo model, we compared the developmental and molecular effects of negatively charged (PS-COOH), positively charged (PS-NH2), and their equal-component mixture (50 nm). No significant mortality was observed across 0.1 to 10 ppm, whereas the lowest tested concentration (0.1 ppm) impaired growth and brain development without significantly increasing mortality. An IA-informed reference-response comparison showed that mixture effects were generally attenuated relative to reference responses derived from the experimentally tested single-particle treatments. Brain transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed distinct surface-chemistry-dependent responses: PS-COOH primarily affected extracellular matrix and glycan-related processes, whereas PS-NH2 altered synaptic, immune, and protein-quality-control pathways. The mixture induced the greatest number of DEGs; this broader omics response does not translate into higher phenotypic toxicity. DIABLO identified treatment-associated RNA-protein covariance, while reference-response comparisons indicated predominantly attenuated molecular responses among statistically supported deviations. Our findings demonstrate that coexposure to oppositely functionalized nanoplastics can reshape developmental and molecular responses during embryonic development.</jats:p>

title: Efficient Water Resistance via High-Spin-State Manganese Species in Low-Temperature NH 3 -SCR

affiliation.name: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics , , Jiangning, ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Development of highly efficient catalysts for low-temperature NH3–SCR remains a significant challenge, especially in the presence of high concentrations of water vapor. Herein, we have engineered a unique MnCeO2-TDA catalyst with high-spin manganese species by using electron-donating thiophene groups, achieving an excellent NO conversion of over 93% at 160 °C and under 60,000 mL·g–1·h–1 conditions in the higher water vapor of 10–20 vol %. Experimental and theoretical calculations demonstrate that, due to, asymmetrically occupied eg orbitals, high-spin Mn3+ triggers a strong Jahn–Teller distortion, which greatly decreases the O2 dissociation energy (from 2.837 to 1.979 eV) and coactivates O2 and H2O to form the *OOH oxidative species. This enhanced redox ability facilitates NO oxidation and the “fast SCR” reaction, leading to excellent deNOx efficiency under higher levels of water vapor at low temperatures. This work offers a new approach to modulating the spin state of active centers to enhance water resistance in flue gas purification.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Microbial-explicit soil carbon models offer mechanistic representations of soil carbon turnover, but their application to the field remains limited, which is commonly attributed to the scarce microbial observations. However, usually there are significant mismatches between model data requirements and the diverse data availability of field observations, which may greatly affect the uncertainty of soil carbon models and have been largely overlooked. Here, we developed a unified framework that systematically quantified how the field observation type, sampling frequency, and measurement uncertainty jointly constrained model parameters and long-term predictions of three representative microbial-explicit soil carbon models. We quantified how well observations of soil carbon stocks, soil respiration, microbial biomass carbon, and functional gene abundance can reduce the parameter and prediction uncertainties across a comprehensive set of field scenarios. High-frequency, low-error soil respiration observations, when combined with soil carbon measurements, dominated uncertainty reduction across carbon pools, while interestingly, microbial observations only provided conditional improvements for microbial and enzyme-related states. More microbial data did not necessarily yield more effective calibration information, and improvements in prediction accuracy required microbial observations with sufficiently small measurement errors. The unified quantitative framework would also help to design a data strategy when developing new soil carbon models to accurately predict soil carbon cycling.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>It remains unclear whether prenatal heat exposure is associated with newborn metabolic profiles. Therefore, based on 4714 mother–infant pairs in Shanghai, we aimed to investigate the trimester-specific associations of prenatal heat exposure with neonatal amino acid (AA) and acylcarnitine (AC) profiles. Heat exposure was defined using the 90th percentile of trimester-specific temperature distributions from the ERA5-Land data set. For AAs, glutamate showed consistently positive associations across three trimesters, whereas phenylalanine, tyrosine, leucine, arginine, and citrulline showed consistently negative associations; other AAs exhibited trimester-specific patterns. For ACs, C2, C4, and C16 showed consistently negative associations, while a chain-length-dependent pattern was observed: short-chain ACs were predominantly negatively associated, whereas most medium- and long-chain ACs reversed to positive associations in the second and third trimesters. Network topology analysis revealed stronger metabolite correlation structures in the heat-exposed group across all trimesters, with AA-AC pairs accounting for the largest proportion of differential correlations. Distributed lag nonlinear models suggested susceptible windows at gestational weeks 10–17 and 25–27 for AAs, and weeks 8–14 and 26–34 for ACs. Overall, prenatal heat exposure was significantly associated with multiple neonatal AAs and ACs, with distinct trimester-specific patterns and a denser intermetabolite correlation network in the heat-exposed group.</jats:p>

Acetylcholine Receptor

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Insecticides targeting nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) are used because of their high neuroactive efficacy. However, they can also exert substantial toxic pressure on nontarget aquatic invertebrates. A previous study suggested that irreversible receptor binding is the main driver of thiacloprid bioaccumulation. To determine whether the observed elimination resistance applies to other nAChR-binding insecticides and species, this study investigates five compounds from different substance classes that target nAChRs. Using the two amphipod species, Hyalella azteca and Gammarus pulex, toxicokinetic experiments were combined with assessing receptor binding in vivo and in vitro. The three N-cyanoamidines and N-nitroguanidine neonicotinoids (thiacloprid, acetamiprid, and imidacloprid) and the metabolite imidacloprid-olefin showed resistance toward elimination (i.e., over 15 days of depuration in both amphipod species). This observation could be well described by a two-compartment toxicokinetic (TK)-receptor model (&gt;0.89 R2) with integrated irreversible binding. In contrast, the butenolide flupyradifurone was fully eliminated, and the organic biocide spinosad was eliminated significantly but slowly, both fitted well with a one-compartment TK model (&gt;0.71 R2). These findings demonstrate that receptor-binding specificity and affinity are highly compound class dependent. Although no direct link between receptor binding and acute toxicity could be established, elimination resistance indicates a risk for delayed, sublethal effects that should be critically considered in regulatory risk assessment.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Condensation sink (CS) from atmospheric pre-existing particles is a crucial limiting factor for the occurrence of new particle formation (NPF). However, intense NPF events occur frequently in polluted urban areas despite high CS levels. Here, to address this discrepancy, we introduce an efficiency coefficient ε (ε = CSeff/CScal) to quantify the CS efficiency of pre-existing particles toward gaseous H2SO4, where CScal was calculated under the assumption of irreversible uptake. Results demonstrate that ε strongly depends on hygroscopicity and chemical compositions of particles. Under dry conditions, the ε of pure organic particles was less than that of pure inorganic particles, but high humidity increased ε for both. For mixed organic-inorganic particles, the ε was adjusted together by particle chemical compositions and humidity. Exploratory measurements further revealed a decline in CS efficiency for gaseous HIO3. Incorporating ε into field data and models improves cluster survival predictions and sub-3-nm particle formation simulations, potentially explaining the NPF mystery in megacities under high CS and leading to more accurate modeling of NPF impacts.</jats:p>

title:
Beyond Equilibrium:
Tracing Redox-Driven Pathways
That Shape Aqueous and Mineral Chemistry

affiliation.name: EMPA, Laboratory for Concrete and Asphalt , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Numerous aqueous and geochemical systems host elements in multiple redox states, with wide ranging implications such as their influence on the formation/dissolution of minerals, water toxicity, and nutrient cycling. To uncover governing mechanisms and complex chemical interactions in geochemical systems, reactive-transport models have increasingly gained importance. However, their predictive capabilities remain limited because existing approaches struggle to accurately account for the full complexities of redox reactions. Here, we develop a reactive-transport framework that leverages recent advances in thermodynamic modeling, speciation chemistry, and redox kinetics. Distinct from traditional models, we uniquely treat redox kinetics along with transport as transient phenomena, decoupled from Gibbs free energy minimization. By ensuring ionic concentrations are governed by nonequilibrium rate laws, this approach allows predicting the tempo-spatial distribution of speciation and precipitation of species across oxidation states. We illustrate the versatility of our framework through two case studies: manganese speciation in natural waters and the fate of dissolved iron in aqueous/porous media. Our framework significantly enhances the modeling of a diverse range of redox-sensitive environments.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Biochar amendment represents a promising in situ strategy for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) mitigation, yet its performance under realistic field conditions remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluated PFAS fate in soil–plant–leachate systems under irrigation-water- and biosolids-derived contamination settings. Pinewood biochar (PBC) significantly (P = 0.05) reduced PFAS leaching and plant uptake more so than biosolids-derived biochar (BBC), driven by its higher point of zero charge (PZC), C/H and C/O ratios, and specific surface area, with the strongest mitigation observed for PFHxS and PFOA. Air oxidation and iron oxide modification of PBC further suppressed short-chain PFAS accumulation in plants. Among the tested materials, air-oxidized PBC exhibited the highest mitigation efficiency (ME), reducing leaf bioconcentration factors (BCFs) of PFHxS and PFOA by 1328.5-fold and 285.3-fold, respectively, and suppressing perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA) accumulation by 150.8-fold, attributable to enhanced surface area, electrostatic attraction, and hydrogen-bonding interactions. Dissolved organic matter (DOM) released from biosolids increased the mobility of PFBA, PFBS, PFOA, and PFHxS while reducing the bioavailability and translocation of PFNA and PFOS. Collectively, this work demonstrates that PFAS mitigation by biochar is governed by molecular structures, input pathways, and DOM interactions, providing mechanistic insight for targeted biochar deployment in PFAS-impacted agroecosystems.</jats:p>

title:
Divergent Catalytic
Strategies of Group-6 Propane
Monooxygenases in Propane-Stimulated 1,4-Dioxane Biodegradation
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Group-6 propane monooxygenases (PRMs) catalyze the initial oxidation of 1,4-dioxane (dioxane), a widespread contaminant of emerging concern. Because their expression can be induced by propane, an inexpensive and readily deliverable substrate, PRM-containing microorganisms offer a distinct advantage for propane-based biostimulation strategies targeting dioxane removal. However, functional differences among PRMs from the three major phylogenetic clusters remain poorly understood. Here, three PRMs from Mycobacterium dioxanotrophicus PH-06, Mycobacterium marinum E11, and Mycobacterium sp. ENV421, representing phylogenetic clusters, PRM-I, PRM-II, and PRM-III, respectively, were heterologously expressed in Mycolicibacterium smegmatis mc2155. ENV421 PRM-III exhibited low substrate affinity but high catalytic capacity toward both dioxane and propane, and moderate resistance to chlorinated solvent inhibition. In contrast, E11 PRM-II displayed high affinity but lower capacity and greater inhibitor sensitivity. PH-06 PRM-I showed comparatively stronger activity toward dioxane than propane relative to the other PRMs. Protein structure analysis suggested that variation in substrate affinity and catalytic turnover is consistent with differences in active-site pocket hydrophobicity, rigidity, and catalytic geometry. Phylogenetic and compositional analyses further suggested horizontal transfer in Clusters I and III. Together, these results highlight substantial functional diversity among group-6 PRMs and offer mechanistic insights for optimizing microbial populations for effective propane-stimulated bioremediation of dioxane.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The widespread use of Aqueous Film-Forming Foams (AFFF) has left thousands of contaminated “hotspots” across North America. In Canada, only 25 per-/polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are regulated in drinking water at 30 ng/L. In the present study, cyclic ion mobility–tandem mass spectrometry (cIMS-MS2) was used to identify 17 regulated and 52 unregulated PFAS in surface waters near a former firefighting training facility in Atlantic Canada, including 6 new PFAS that have not been previously reported in environmental waters: hydrido-ketone-5:2-fluorotelomer sulfonate (FTS), ketone-8:2-FTS, unsaturated 8:2-FTS, N-methyl-perfluorohexane sulfonamido sulfinate, N-methyl-perfluorooctane sulfonamido sulfinate, and perfluorohexane sulfonamido propionate. Semi-quantitation of unregulated PFAS was enabled by a machine-learning model validated using a set of 21 targeted PFAS (R2 &gt; 0.95). The total concentration of PFAS declined from 2500 ng/L to 364 ng/L as the surface water entered the North Atlantic approximately 5 km away from the hotspot. Seven of forty-two drinking water wells located along a 5 km transect from the source were characterized by exceedances between 30 and 191 ng/L. Twenty-seven PFAS were identified in the wells, including 13 that are unregulated and 5 that result from (bio)transformation of AFFF. While the fraction of unregulated PFAS was low (&lt;18%), these transformation products may inform forensic studies aimed at establishing links between the source of pollution and its receptors.</jats:p>

title:
Elevated Outdoor

Formation and Growth Indoors
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ultrafine particles and submicron aerosol mass negatively impact human health; while indoor primary sources are known, secondary aerosol formation from oxidation of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) is an important, but less understood, exposure source. Previous studies have suggested that indoor new particle formation (NPF) and growth are ozone-limited. However, we find that in an authentic aged unoccupied office in a region with high outdoor O3 concentrations, sufficient O3 is transported indoors that NPF and growth are instead limited by the availability of VOCs. Mechanical ventilation continuously supplies O3 in the summertime and sustains the subsequent growth so that particle growth rates upon the addition of limonene range from 20 to 100 nm h–1─rates 1–2 orders of magnitude greater than those observed outdoors. Additionally, we observe meaningful mass contributions from the growth of newly formed particles. Household use of limonene-containing products in rooms with elevated ozone─either from ozone-producing remediation and germicidal UV technologies, or during outdoor ozone exceedance events─will produce ultrafine particles and increase particle mass. The effect of ventilated O3 from outdoors on particle formation and growth highlights the value of continued efforts to reduce outdoor O3 pollution for moderating both indoor and outdoor sources of secondary pollutants.</jats:p>

title:
Toward
Recreating the Breath of Cities in the Atmospheric
Simulation Chamber SAPHIR

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Atmospheric simulation chambers are essential for studying oxidation processes, yet many experiments rely on single-precursor systems at concentrations that limit their representativeness for the chemical complexity of urban air. Here, we present a framework linking emission inventories, chamber experiments, and field observations by constructing emission fingerprints of major urban sources, including vegetation, volatile chemical products, cooking emissions, and gasoline and diesel exhaust. Applied during the CHANEL campaign in the SAPHIR outdoor chamber, these fingerprints advanced toward reproducing gas-phase mixtures representative of Los Angeles (gasoline-dominated traffic), a diesel-dominated city, and a future low-vehicle-emission scenario. The resulting mixtures generated peroxy-to-hydroperoxy radical ratios (RO2/HO2) close to unity, bimolecular RO2 lifetimes comparable with urban atmospheric observations, although lower NO levels favored RO2 + HO2 over RO2 + NO reactions. Comparison with aircraft measurements over Los Angeles using ammonium (NH4+) chemical ionization mass spectrometry showed reasonable agreement, with 465 organic product ions detected in both data sets, representing 78% of the product ions observed in the ambient air. Furthermore, 87% of common product ions agreed within a factor of 3 of the linear correlation, demonstrating that chamber experiments can capture key aspects of both atmospherically relevant radical chemistry and the oxidation product diversity of urban air.</jats:p>

title:
Novel
Insight into Organoarsenic Degradation and Inorganic
Arsenic Sequestration in Ferrate Treatment: Unraveling the Role of
Active Fe–As Complexes at the Molecular Level

affiliation.name: Xi’an University of Architecture and Technology , , ,
Xi’an University of Architecture and Technology , , ,
Xi’an University of Architecture and Technology , , ,
Xi’an University of Architecture and Technology , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Efficiently removing organoarsenic contaminants like p-Aminophenylarsonic acid (pASA) with their toxic inorganic byproducts remains a major challenge. Ferrate [Fe(VI)] can oxidize organoarsenic and immobilize inorganic arsenic, but the molecular mechanisms linking these functions are unclear. Here, using theoretical computational spectroscopy and stopped-flow analysis, we identified a critical pathway mediated by Fe(V/IV)–O-As(III) intermediates (INTs) that bridges oxidative degradation and heterogeneous sequestration. X-band EPR further confirmed the INTs (g-factors = 2.006, 1.928, 1.712), with rhombic peaks and quadruple hyperfine splitting. These INTs form barrierlessly between Fe(VI/V) and ·As(III)O(OH)2 released upon C–As bond cleavage in pASA. The thus-formed INTs exhibit superior reactivity to Fe(VI/V/IV), enabling more effective organoarsenic degradation and As(III) oxidation via outer-sphere electron transfer. Additionally, these INTs facilitate highly efficient inner-sphere electron transfer, forming Fe(III/II)–O-As(V) complexes that directly evolve into As-bearing Fe nanoparticles via Fe–O–As bond formation, a process with a lower energy barrier. The abundance of INTs during pASA degradation can be regulated by modulating Fe(VI) decomposition kinetics using common reagents: H2O2 accelerates and NaClO delays Fe(VI) decomposition. The Fe(VI)/NaClO system achieved 88% total As removal, higher than the 72% for Fe(VI)/H2O2 and 78% for Fe(VI) alone, and exhibited enhanced As–Fe coordination, indicating improved sequestration. Overall, this work reveals a pivotal mechanistic bridge in metalloid contaminant removal, offering new insights for designing oxidation-sequestration synergy in environmental remediation.</jats:p>

title: Establishment of a Novel Alternative Method Using the Gobiocypris rarus AhR for Toxicity Testing of the Dioxin-like Potency of Halogenated Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Halogenated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (HPAHs) often exhibit distinct toxicity and mechanisms relative to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), yet most remain unassessed, particularly for dioxin-like effects mediated by the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR). This study characterized three rare minnow AhRs and established an efficient AhR-activation screening assay (using graAhR2, EC50 = 2.53 nM and Z′ factor = 0.58), and evaluated 40 HPAHs/PAHs with preliminary activity screening and ecotoxicity considered. HPAHs showed a median IC50 of 1.15 × 10–4 M for cellular viability (parent PAHs: 4.29 × 10–4 M), indicating greater cellular toxicity. Nine compounds were AhR-active. Notably, halogenated fluorene and pyrene exhibited AhR activation, whereas the parent did not. 4-bromobenz[a]anthracene exhibited 2028-fold higher activation potency than the parent. Acute toxicity (cell viability IC50) and AhR activation potency (EC50) exhibited a weak correlation, R2 = 0.21 and P = 0.22 in COS-7 cells, implying little AhR contribution to acute toxicity. All HPAHs/PAHs shared a similar binding direction within the AhR. AhR-active compounds possessed greater affinity than inactive ones (P = 0.0032). For instance, in fluorene-based HPAHs, a binding pose more similar to 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD) may confer stronger activation potency. The results support the need for a tiered risk evaluation of HPAHs, e.g., considering acute and long-term aspects, and integrating dioxin-like potency into relevant regulatory frameworks, e.g., the toxic equivalency factor (TEF) or similar ones.</jats:p>

title:
Decadal Biochar
Legacy Stabilizes Paddy Soil Carbon
by Reshaping Redox-Driven Reactive Oxygen Species Dynamics
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Biochar (BC) displays great potential in stabilizing soil organic carbon, yet its decadal legacy for carbon preservation under redox oscillations remains unclear. The study comprehensively investigated how decadal BC (D-BC) application restrained carbon mineralization of paddy soil via reshaping reactive oxygen species (ROS) dynamics. In situ fluorescence imaging and quantification results showed that D-BC soil inhibited hydroxyl radical (•OH) generation by 22.3% than fresh BC (F-BC) input soil, but elevating hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and superoxide (O2•–) accumulation by 36.2% and 25.4% during redox oscillation, respectively. This resulted from its weakened microbial iron reduction and the lower reactivity of Fe(II), which significantly limited Fenton reactions. In contrast, a shift in the microbial community to redox-adapted taxa, lower catalase activity, and enriched dissolved inorganic carbon collectively facilitated the biogenic origin of H2O2 in D-BC soil. Scavenging and correlation analyses revealed that reduced •OH generation led to net suppression in CO2 emission from D-BC soil by &gt;30% via upregulating the enzymatic latch, while enhanced H2O2 accumulation imposed oxidative stress on carbon-degrading microbes. Laboratory verifications confirmed the roles of surface oxidation and persistent free radical attenuation of aged BC in ROS redistribution. The failure of decadal straw (D-Straw) return to reproduce these phenomena suggested that the decadal BC legacy stemmed from a particular redox impact, rather than exogenous carbon input alone. The findings uncovered a new mechanism of BC-induced carbon stability, advancing understanding of the carbon cycle within redox-dynamic zones.</jats:p>

title:
Ice
Converts Phenols
into Persistent Mineral-Bound
Polymers
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Freezing fundamentally alters how minerals transform dissolved phenols in cold environments. As water freezes, solutes are excluded from the crystal lattice and concentrated into microscopic pockets of unfrozen liquid, creating reaction conditions far more extreme than those of bulk solution. Here, we compare catechol oxidation on a key soil manganese oxide under freeze–thaw versus room-temperature conditions. Freezing redirects products from soluble humic-like substances to thermally stable, mineral-bound polymers. Freeze–thaw conditions removed over 50% of dissolved organic carbon within 24 h compared to less than 10% at room temperature, with solid-phase carbon increasing over 50-fold. The attenuation of the effect with increasing salinity is consistent with freeze-concentration as a key driver and indicates that the pathway should be strongest in freshwater and low-salinity frozen environments. Freeze–thaw conditions also converted preformed soluble products into mineral-bound forms, demonstrating that the process operates on a range of substrates. These findings reveal an unrecognized abiotic carbon stabilization pathway that could operate when microbial decomposition is suppressed by freezing with direct implications for carbon dynamics in permafrost and seasonally frozen environments.</jats:p>

title:
Why
Can Cross-End Point Transfer Fail in Computational
Toxicology? Diagnosing Decision-Structure Incompatibility across 13
End Points under Scaffold-Held-Out Evaluation
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cross-end point information sharing may improve toxicity prediction when labeled data are limited, but biologically related end points are not necessarily predictively compatible. We evaluated transfer strategies across 13 toxicity end points using scaffold-disjoint repeated cross-validation with strict leakage control. The benchmark compared data-level pooling with higher-level approaches, including stacking, multitask learning, model-agnostic meta-learning, and frozen-encoder feature augmentation (FEFA). Direct cross-prediction between different end points was generally weak, with a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.525 across 156 ordered end point pairs, indicating limited standalone portability of end point-specific decision rules. Global data merging reduced macro-average ROC-AUC by 0.0287 relative to end point-specific baselines, whereas several higher-level approaches produced modest gains. The strongest macro-average improvements were observed for stacking (+0.0101 ROC-AUC) and FEFA (+0.0070), although effects varied substantially among end points. Additional decision-structure and representation analyses were consistent with transfer performance being strategy- and target-dependent rather than determined by biological relatedness alone. These findings support leakage-controlled, end point-specific evaluation when using cross-end point learning for chemical toxicity assessment and caution against indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous toxicity data.</jats:p>

title:
Volatile and Semi-volatile
Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl
Substances (PFAS): Air–Water Partitioning, Atmospheric Emissions,
and Environmental Fate and Transport

affiliation.name: Jacobs , 9304 Coachway , , ,
place: Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States, 27516

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Volatile and semi-volatile per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (V/SV-PFAS) represent a class of PFAS that can partition into the gas phase, enabling atmospheric transport and inhalation exposure pathways that remain poorly understood. Recognizing that air–water partitioning is a fundamental determinant of environmental volatility, this review critically evaluates the current understanding of air–water partitioning coefficients (Kaw), atmospheric emissions, and subsurface occurrence and associated vapor intrusion (VI) risks of V/SV-PFAS. Experimentally determined Kaw values are compiled, highlighting variability spanning multiple orders of magnitude and uncertainties that may arise from limitations of conventional measurement techniques or differences in experimental methodologies. Recent advances, such as thermodynamic cycle methods, are assessed for their potential to expand the range of measurable V/SV-PFAS. Field observations from major atmospheric emission sources, including landfills, wastewater treatment plants, PFAS manufacturing facilities, vadose-zone soil gas at contaminated sites, and indoor environments, are evaluated. Fluorotelomer alcohols dominate V/SV-PFAS profiles, with concentrations of up to 105–106 ng/m3 in landfill and soil gas, 103–104 ng/m3 in industrial indoor air, 103–104 pg/m3 in ambient air near source regions, and 103 to 106 pg/m3 in indoor environments. Addressing critical knowledge gaps in air–water partitioning, source characterization, and subsurface fate and transport is essential for improving V/SV-PFAS exposure assessment and developing effective management strategies.</jats:p>

title: Issue Editorial Masthead
Issue Publication Information
Inland Migration Space Requirements for Maintaining Blue Carbon Stocks after Spartina Eradication under Accelerating Sea Level Rise
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>China’s nationwide Spartina alterniflora eradication program across 18,000 km of coastline aims to restore native biodiversity, but removing these carbon-rich invasive stands is estimated to release 21.4 Mt CO2. This challenge is compounded by accelerating sea level rise, which threatens the native replacements meant to restore blue carbon functions, and current restoration approaches lack systematic strategies to address both pressures. We coupled species distribution modeling with the Sea Level Affecting Marshes Model (SLAMM) to project the performance of two posteradication restoration strategies─Environmental Suitability (ES, prioritizing habitat preferences) and Optimized Carbon Stock (CS, prioritizing high-carbon species)─under SSP1–2.6 and SSP5–8.5 through 2100, and quantified the minimum inland migration area required to sustain a target carbon stock (2.16 Tg C). Across projections for 2060 and 2100, tidal marshes outside seawalls are projected to lose 23–50% of their area, with carbon stocks declining 12–51% relative to 2021 levels. The CS strategy maintained 6–16% higher carbon stocks than ES. Mainting the target carbon stock required 31–157 km2 of inland migration space, with CS’s advantage over ES in reducing migration requirements narrowing from 37% under SSP1-2.6 (2060) to 4% under SSP5-8.5 (2100). These results show that management strategies lose effectiveness under extreme climate conditions, underscoring the value of early intervention under low-emission scenarios, and offer practical migration-space targets for coastal planning wherever invasive species control intersects with accelerating environmental change.</jats:p>

title:
Selective Destabilization
of Mineral-Protected Organic
Carbon Accompanies Iron Reduction across a Coastal Wetland Salinity
Gradient

affiliation.name: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences , , ,
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences , , ,
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Climate-driven seawater intrusion is intensifying salinization in coastal wetlands, but its consequences for the stability of sediment organic carbon (OC) remain poorly constrained. Here, we combined field observations along a natural salinity gradient with spectroscopic and mineralogical analyses, mineral sorption–desorption experiments, and manipulative incubations to examine the stability of mineral-protected OC. Salt-marsh sediments contained 9.23% less OC than freshwater sediments, with a disproportionate difference in reactive iron-bound OC (FeR-OC). Across the 36 independent field plots, FeR-OC represented 9.80–22.95% of total OC, while the FW–SM FeR-OC difference was numerically equivalent to 64.28% of the corresponding bulk-OC difference. This disproportionate response was associated with a shift from reactive Fe(III)-bearing phases toward Fe(II)-rich products, as well as a weakening of mineral protection, supported by spectroscopic, mineralogical, and geochemical evidence. In salt-marsh incubations, molybdate addition decreased FeR-OC mobilization by 39.51%, identifying a molybdate-sensitive contribution consistent with the sulfate-reduction branch. Together, these results support an iron-unlocking pathway in sulfate-rich coastal wetlands, in which Fe reduction weakens mineral protection and mobilizes previously stabilized OC. This mechanism identifies iron-mediated mineral protection as an important geochemical vulnerability of blue carbon under increasing seawater influence, while the subsequent mineralization, export, or recapture of mobilized OC remains unresolved.</jats:p>

title:
Putting Large Language
Models into Environmental Context
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed information interaction, yet their application in environmental science and engineering (ESE) is hindered by multimodal data formats, dynamic context requirements, and hallucination risks. To transition from general-purpose models to domain expert agentic systems, this Perspective introduces a three-pillar framework for ESE-LLMs: domain perception, knowledge grounding, and action capability. Implementing these capabilities introduces potential pitfalls such as geographic representation bias, catastrophic forgetting, and source authenticity vulnerabilities, which require strategic model blending and careful data curation to overcome. Furthermore, rigorous evaluation must extend beyond standard knowledge benchmarks to systematically assess factuality, fairness, consistency, and safety using both human and automated metrics. Finally, we present a decision-guided deployment workflow that helps researchers in ESE fields integrate LLMs into their workflow. Ultimately, achieving trustworthy environmental intelligence relies on continuous evaluation, robust governance, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration to safely deploy agentic ESE-LLMs for high-stakes environmental challenges.</jats:p>

title:
Catalyst
or Bystander? Disentangling True Catalytic
Effects from Confounding Phenomena in Ozone-Based Wastewater Treatment

affiliation.name: UNSW Centre for Transformational Environmental Technologies , Environmental Protection Technology Industrial Park , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Heterogeneous catalytic ozonation has generated thousands of publications over two decades, with these publications articulating a consistent narrative: catalysts enhance ozone decomposition, generate hydroxyl radicals (or other reactive species), and improve contaminant removal beyond that achievable by use of ozone alone. Despite this narrative, performance gains demonstrated at laboratory scale are routinely inconsistent and poorly reproduced at pilot and industrial scale. This perspective argues that the field suffers from a systematic attribution problem with observed enhancements frequently misattributed to catalytic activity when, instead, they arise from gas–liquid mass transfer modification, pH effects, and/or metal leaching driving homogeneous reactions. Using quantitative modeling, we further demonstrate that faster catalyst-mediated reaction kinetics alone may not translate into meaningful process-level benefits, particularly in full-scale reactors where relatively long hydraulic retention times and constraints on O3 gas–liquid mass transfer can diminish the advantage of kinetic acceleration. A sustained catalytic advantage at scale, therefore, requires not only kinetic acceleration but also more efficient utilization of ozone, an important distinction that has received limited attention in the HCO literature. Based on these findings, we propose a framework that will assist in distinguishing true catalytic pathways from various confounders and will help establish process-relevant benefit of HCO at scale. Overall, this perspective establishes a more rigorous evidentiary basis for translating catalytic activity into reliable wastewater treatment performance.</jats:p>

title:
Fate
of Perfluoroalkyl Acids during Thermal Regeneration
of Hydrotalcite
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Calcined hydrotalcite (cgHT) is a promising PFAS adsorbent because it may enable PFAS destruction and sorbent regeneration at reduced temperatures. This study evaluated the thermal behavior of PFOS and PFOA adsorbed on cgHT at temperatures ranging from 125 to 550 °C and compared it with their behavior on sand (a reference carrier). Targeted PFAS, total fluorine, and fluoride analyses were used to quantify fluorine-containing products and establish fluorine mass balances across the solid, liquid, and gas phases. For both PFOS and PFOA, more than 75% of the initial fluorine remained associated with cgHT in an unextractable, likely inorganic form. In contrast, less than 40% of the initial fluorine was recovered as fluoride overall from the sand experiments, with less than 6% retained as solid-phase fluoride. Fewer types of volatile organic fluorine byproducts were detected in the cgHT experiments than in the sand experiments. Enhanced PFOS and PFOA degradation on cgHT may involve reactions with the bentonite binder, or the magnesium oxide and water generated from cgHT at elevated temperature. Adsorption and thermal regeneration performance did not change significantly over three adsorption–regeneration cycles. The results support further evaluation of cgHT as a thermally regenerable PFAS sorbent.</jats:p>

title:
Fusion-DeepRSM
for Satellite-Derived PM2.5 Estimation and Precursor Sensitivity
Prediction

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate estimation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and characterization of precursor-response relationships are crucial for human health protection and air quality management. However, current approaches remain limited by the high computational cost and uncertainties of chemical transport models (CTMs), as well as the sample imbalance and limited interpretability of observation-based machine learning methods. Here, we developed Fusion-DeepRSM, an observation-constrained extension of the Deep Learning Response Surface Model (DeepRSM) framework that integrates CTM simulations, multisource satellite observations, and ground-based measurements to derive spatially continuous PM2.5 concentrations and characterize precursor-PM2.5 response relationships. Results from ground-based observations and CTM-based testbed experiments show that Fusion-DeepRSM effectively alleviates the sample imbalance in conventional models and mitigates PM2.5 overestimation in rural regions, with an average reduction of 4.13 μg/m3 while maintaining high predictive accuracy (R2 = 0.872 and RMSE = 11.82 μg/m3). In addition, Fusion-DeepRSM successfully quantifies precursor-PM2.5 response relationships, revealing pronounced seasonal and regional heterogeneity consistent with established atmospheric chemistry understanding. With high computational efficiency, Fusion-DeepRSM further quantifies the effects of meteorological conditions and pollutant concentrations on PM2.5 variability. During the nationwide PM2.5 decline from 2020 to 2023, unfavorable meteorology partially offset pollutant-related improvements (+1.2 versus −1.8 μg/m3), while changes in precursor pollutant conditions played an important role in the February 2023 PM2.5 rebound in the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region. These findings demonstrate the strong potential of Fusion-DeepRSM for air quality modeling and region-specific pollution mitigation.</jats:p>

title:
Greenhouse Gas and
Ammonia Emission Factors from Raw
and Digested Cattle Slurry: A Field-Based Synthesis for Cattle Systems

affiliation.name: Bioeconomy Science Institute Maiangi Taiao, AgResearch Group, Lincoln Research Centre , ,
Bioeconomy Science Institute Maiangi Taiao, AgResearch Group, Lincoln Research Centre , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Anaerobic digestion (AD) of cattle slurry is widely promoted as a manure-management strategy, yet its effects on greenhouse gas (GHG) and ammonia (NH3) emissions remain uncertain. This review provides the first field-based synthesis of paired methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), and NH3 emission factors (EFs) from raw and digested cattle slurry during storage and land application. A total of 98 paired observations from 16 studies were analyzed using paired bootstrap geometric mean ratios. AD reduced dry matter, volatile solids, and carbon content while increasing total ammoniacal nitrogen (TAN) and pH. Consequently, digestate CH4 EFs during storage were 51% lower than those of raw slurry (p = 0.001). In contrast, NH3–N EFs increased by 63% during storage (p = 0.071) and by 40% following land application (p = 0.003). However, TAN-normalized NH3 EFs did not differ between manure types, suggesting similar volatilization potential. AD had no significant effect on N2O EFs. A system-level analysis showed that AD reduced total GHG emissions across the storage-to-land-application continuum by 49%, although this benefit was partially offset by increased NH3 losses. These findings identify AD as an effective CH4 mitigation strategy for cattle slurry when combined with targeted NH3 abatement measures to maximize environmental benefits.</jats:p>
